# Word command reference

Every built-in Word command, with what Word and Microsoft say about it: its macro name and description,
its keys, where it sits on the ribbon, on the right-click menus and on Word's legacy menus, the built-in
dialog it opens and that dialog's arguments, and how its ribbon controls changed from Office 2013 to
Microsoft 365.

Generated 2026-10-23 on Word for Microsoft 365, version 16.0 build 16.0.19127, Windows 11, English (United
States) UI. Anything read from Word reflects that install, including its add-ins and its Normal template.

## How each part was resolved

Word was driven over COM from PowerShell (`New-Object -ComObject Word.Application`, hidden, on a new blank
document). Every key-binding probe below was made with `CustomizationContext` set to that unsaved document,
which was then closed without saving, so Normal.dotm was never changed.

### Commands and keys: ListCommands

`Application.ListCommands(ListAllCommands:=True)` is the built-in ListCommands macro with *All Word
commands* chosen. It writes a new document holding one table, which was read cell by cell. This Word's
table has three columns, command name, modifiers and key; a command bound to several keys has one row per
binding. It gave 2159 rows: 1690 distinct named commands and 354 rows named only
`Office Drawing Command`. The Menu column older Words wrote is gone.

### Macro names

ListCommands gives display names (`Save As`); Word runs commands by macro name (`FileSaveAs`), and has no
call from one to the other. Each macro name here was confirmed by Word one of two ways:

- **By key.** For a command with a key, `Application.FindKey(KeyCode).Command` returns the macro name
  bound to that key. Key codes were built from `WdKey` values: Ctrl 512, Shift 256, Alt 1024, letters and
  digits as their ASCII codes, F1-F12 as 112-123, and the virtual-key codes for the named keys
  (`Page Down` 34, `[` 219 and so on). All 254 keyed rows resolved.
- **By name.** Otherwise the display name with its spaces taken out was offered to
  `KeyBindings.Add(wdKeyCategoryCommand, Name, Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F1)`. Word accepts only a real command, and
  `FindKey` on the probe key then reports its canonical spelling; the binding was cleared after each.

Together they resolve 1147 of the 1690 distinct display names. The rest are left blank:
their macro name is not the display name run together.

### Descriptions

`WordBasic.MacroDesc$(Name)`, called through `Type.InvokeMember` on the `Application.WordBasic` object, is
the description Word's Macros dialog shows for a Word command. It answers only for a macro name, so it was
asked of every macro name gathered above, from the ribbon, from the dialogs and from the documented
shortcuts. `WordBasic.CountMacros` / `MacroName$`, which once listed Word's commands, return nothing in
this Word, and `MacroDesc$` returns nothing once key bindings have been probed in the same session, so it
was run in a session of its own.

### Ribbon and right-click menus: Office Fluent UI command identifiers

Microsoft publishes every control of Word's ribbon, Backstage, Quick Access Toolbar and right-click menus,
with its control type, tab set, tab, group or menu, parent controls and Policy ID:

- Repository: https://github.com/OfficeDev/office-fluent-ui-command-identifiers (MIT), read from a local
  clone at commit `b230a0d` (2024-03-18).
- Files: `wordcontrols.xlsx` under `Office 2013`, `Office 2016`, `Office 2019` and `Microsoft 365/` `Semi-Annual
  Enterprise Channel`, `Monthly Enterprise Channel` and `Current Channel`. The workbooks were read as Open XML
  (shared strings and sheet XML); 2013 and 2016 carry a *Tertiary Parent Control* column the later ones lack.
- The Current Channel file is the one this Word matches, and is what every location below is read from;
  the others feed only [Ribbon changes across versions](#ribbon-changes-across-versions).

Tab sets, tabs, groups, menus and parents are given in the sheets as idMso names (`TabHome`, `GroupFont`);
they are shown here by the label Word gives them, from `CommandBars.GetLabelMso`, or by the idMso where Word
has no label for it.

### Ribbon details from Word

For every idMso in any of the six sheets, `Application.CommandBars` gave:

- `GetLabelMso`: the label; `GetScreentipMso`: the ScreenTip title; `GetSupertipMso`: the longer description;
- `GetEnabledMso`, `GetPressedMso`, `GetVisibleMso`: the state on a new blank document, cursor at its start.
  Pressed is blank for a control that cannot be pressed.
- `GetImageMso` fails from PowerShell for every control (its `IPictureDisp` does not marshal), so there are
  no icons here.

Which ribbon controls are Word commands was settled the same way as the macro names: every idMso was
offered to `KeyBindings.Add`, and the 271 Word accepts are Word commands, run by that name. A command
takes a control's locations only through that match, never by a name that merely looks alike.

### Legacy command bars

`Application.CommandBars` still holds Word 2003's menus and toolbars (and many of Word's right-click menus
in their old form). Every bar was read (`Name`, `NameLocal`, `Type`, `BuiltIn`, `Visible`, control count),
and every control walked recursively through popups (`Id`, `Type`, `Caption`, `TooltipText`,
`DescriptionText`, `ShortcutText`, `FaceId`, `BuiltIn`, `Visible`, `Enabled`). A control's `Id` is the
Policy ID in the Fluent UI sheets, which is how a ribbon control, and through it a Word command, gets its
legacy menus.

### Built-in dialogs: Microsoft Learn and Word

From Microsoft's VBA documentation, licensed CC BY 4.0 (https://github.com/MicrosoftDocs/VBA-Docs, branch
`live`; © Microsoft Corporation, used under https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/):

- `WdWordDialog` enumeration: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/office/vba/api/word.wdworddialog
  (source `api/Word.WdWordDialog.md`): each constant, its value and the arguments it lists;
- `WdWordDialogTab` enumeration: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/office/vba/api/word.wdworddialogtab
  (source `api/Word.WdWordDialogTab.md`);
- Built-in dialog box argument lists:
  https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/office/vba/word/concepts/customizing-word/built-in-dialog-box-argument-lists-word
  (source `word/Concepts/Customizing-Word/built-in-dialog-box-argument-lists-word.md`).

The tables were fetched as markdown from the repository and only their table rows used; `**` and `_`
emphasis was removed. Each enum value was then opened in Word as `Application.Dialogs(Value)` for its
`CommandName` (the Word command the dialog belongs to), `CommandBarId`, `DefaultTab` and `Type`, without
showing it. A value Word refuses is marked with Word's error.

Microsoft Learn's current VBA documentation has no list of WordBasic commands or of their Visual Basic
equivalents (the old *Visual Basic Equivalents for WordBasic Commands* topic was not carried over), so none
is included.

### Keyboard shortcuts: Microsoft Support

*Keyboard shortcuts in Word*,
https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/keyboard-shortcuts-in-word-95ef89dd-7142-4b50-afb2-f762f663ceb2,
fetched 2026-10-23. Only the Windows part was read (up to its first *See also*). That page is not openly
licensed, so its wording is not reproduced: what is kept is each key combination, the section it is listed
under, and what Word itself binds to it. Each combination that names one key chord (alternatives split on
*or*) was turned into a key code and given to `Application.FindKey`; Ribbon KeyTip sequences (`Alt, H, F, O`)
and keys described in prose are listed as written, unresolved.

### Joins, in brief

| From | To | Through |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ListCommands display name | macro name | `FindKey` on the command's key, or `KeyBindings.Add` on the name without spaces |
| macro name | description | `WordBasic.MacroDesc$` |
| macro name | ribbon control | the idMso Word accepts as that command in `KeyBindings.Add` |
| ribbon control | legacy menus | Policy ID = `CommandBarControl.Id` |
| macro name | dialog | `Dialogs(WdWordDialog).CommandName` |
| documented shortcut | macro name | `FindKey` |

## The Office Drawing Command rows

ListCommands names 354 commands only `Office Drawing Command`, with no key. They are the drawing
commands Office shares across its applications, not Word's own, and Word gives them neither a name nor an
ID there. None of the drawing controls' names (`ShapeRectangle`, `ShapeOval`, `ObjectsAlignLeft`) is accepted
by `KeyBindings` as a Word command, so the rows cannot be named one to one. Their real names are among the
[Ribbon controls](#ribbon-controls) whose *Word command* is blank, e.g. `ShapeRectangle`, *Rectangle*,
Policy ID 1111, on the legacy `Drawing > AutoShapes > Basic Shapes` menu.

## Built-in dialogs

235 `WdWordDialog` constants. *Arguments* is the Built-in Dialog Box Argument Lists page, falling back to
the enumeration page's own column; *Command*, *Bar ID*, *Default tab* and *Type* are Word's, from
`Application.Dialogs(Value)`, and *Description* is `MacroDesc$` of that command.

286 entries in the Windows part of *Keyboard shortcuts in Word*. *Word binds* is `FindKey` on each
chord: a macro name for a command (category 1), or the font, style, AutoText or symbol it inserts for the
other categories, blank where Word binds nothing and handles the key itself. *In ListCommands* says whether
ListCommands reported that chord.

| Use function key shortcuts | F1 alone: displays the Word help task pane.Shift+F1: displays or hides context-sensitive help or the Reveal Formatting task pane.Ctrl+F1: displays or hides the ribbon.Alt+F1: moves to the next field.Alt+Shift+F1: moves to the previous field. |  |  |  |  |  |
| Use function key shortcuts | F2 alone: moves the selected text or graphic. Use the arrow keys to place the cursor where you want to move the text or graphic, and then press Enter to move, or press Esc to cancel.Shift+F2: copies the selected text or graphic. Use the arrow keys to place the cursor where you want to copy the text or graphic, and then press Enter to copy, or press Esc to cancel.Ctrl+F2: displays the print preview area on the Print tab in the Backstage view.Alt+Shift+F2: saves the document.Ctrl+Alt+F2: displays the Open dialog box. |  |  |  |  |  |
| Use function key shortcuts | Shift+F3: switches the selected text between upper case, lower case, and title case.Ctrl+F3: cuts the selected content to the Spike. You can cut multiple texts and graphics to the Spike, and paste them as a group to another location.Ctrl+Shift+F3: pastes the contents of the Spike.Alt+F3: creates a new Building Block. |  |  |  |  |  |
| Use function key shortcuts | F4 alone: repeats the last command or action, if possible.Shift+F4: repeats the last Find or Go To action.Ctrl+F4: closes the current document.Alt+F4: closes Word. |  |  |  |  |  |
| Use function key shortcuts | F5 alone: displays the Go To dialog box.Shift+F5: moves the cursor to the last change.Ctrl+Shift+F5: displays the Bookmark dialog box.Alt+F5: restores the document window size. |  |  |  |  |  |
| Use function key shortcuts | F6 alone: switch between the document, task pane, status bar, and ribbon. In a document that has been split, F6 includes the split panes when switching between panes and the task pane.Shift+F6: switches between the document, ribbon, status bar, and task pane.Ctrl+F6: switches to the next document window when more than one document is open.Ctrl+Shift+F6: switches to the previous document window when more than one document is open.Alt+F6: moves from an open dialog box back to the document, for dialog boxes that support this behavior. |  |  |  |  |  |
| Use function key shortcuts | F7 alone: displays the Editor task pane to check spelling and grammar in the document or the selected text.Shift+F7: displays the Thesaurus task pane.Ctrl+Shift+F7: updates the linked information in a Word source document.Alt+F7: finds the next spelling or grammatical error.Alt+Shift+F7: displays the Translator task pane. |  |  |  |  |  |
| Use function key shortcuts | F8 alone: extends the selection. For example, if a word is selected, the selection size is extended to one sentence.Shift+F8: reduces the selection. For example, if a paragraph is selected, the selection size is reduced to one sentence.Ctrl+Shift+F8: turns extend selection mode on and off. In the extend selection mode, the arrow keys extend the selection.Alt+F8: displays the Macro dialog box to create, run, edit, or delete a macro. |  |  |  |  |  |
| Use function key shortcuts | F9 alone: updates the selected fields.Shift+F9: switches between a field code and its result.Ctrl+F9: inserts an empty field.Ctrl+Shift+F9: unlinks the current field.Alt+F9: switches between all field codes and their results.Alt+Shift+F9: runs GOTOBUTTON or MACROBUTTON from a field displaying field results. |  |  |  |  |  |
| Use function key shortcuts | F10 alone: turns KeyTips on or off.Shift+F10: displays the shortcut menu for the selected item.Ctrl+F10: maximizes or restores the document window size.Alt+F10: displays the Selection task pane.Alt+Shift+F10: displays the menu or message for available actions, for example, for pasted text or an AutoCorrect change. |  |  |  |  |  |
| Use function key shortcuts | F11 alone: moves to the next field.Shift+F11: moves to the previous field.Ctrl+F11: locks the current field.Ctrl+Shift+F11: unlocks the current field.Alt+F11: opens the Microsoft Visual Basic for Applications editor, in which you can create a macro using Visual Basic for Applications (VBA). |  |  |  |  |  |
| Use function key shortcuts | F12 alone: displays the Save As dialog box.Shift+F12: saves the document.Ctrl+F12: displays the Open dialog box.Ctrl+Shift+F12: displays the Print tab in the Backstage view.Alt+Shift+F12: selects the Table of Contents button in the Table of Contents container when the container is active. |  |  |  |  |  |

## Ribbon changes across versions

Controls that appear in one sheet and not the one before it, in the order Office 2013, 2016, 2019, then the
Microsoft 365 channels from the slowest (Semi-Annual) to the fastest (Current). A control that stays but
moves is in the second table, which compares Office 2013 with Current Channel.
